"executive_summary": "This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method for producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry. The authors propose a free-solvent mechanochemical process that combines eggshell waste (a food-industry residue rich in calcite, CaCO3) with monobasic potassium dihydrogen phosphate (KH2PO4) to synthesize new phosphate phases, principally K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, aimed at improving the management of phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and calcium (Ca) in soil systems. The central hypothesis is that these mechanochemically derived phosphates act as 'smart release' fertilizers: they delay the bioavailability of the highly soluble P and K (which release rapidly from KH2PO4) while simultaneously enhancing the bioavailability of Ca, which is otherwise extremely slow to release from eggshell CaCO3. The mechanochemical activation is performed in a solvent-free environment using a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7), with the goal of minimizing waste and energy consumption while promoting solid-phase ion migration and new structure formation. The experimental design systematically varied milling time (15 min to 24 h) and milling speed (100 to 600 rpm) to evaluate the acid-base reactions between the precursors. Characterization was performed using X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR MAS), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), with nutrient content determined by acid digestion followed by atomic absorption and colorimetric methods. Nutrient release behavior was evaluated in two complementary systems: a citric acid solution (2 wt%) following the MAPA recommended procedure, and soil-based release essays (both diffusion-zone visualization and aerobic soil conditions). The key results demonstrate that the milled samples exhibit slower release of P and K compared to the KH2PO4 precursor, while showing faster Ca release compared to the eggshell CaCO3 precursor. In soil, the 2 h/600 rpm sample showed a progressive P release reaching 45 mg/kg after 30 days (15% of total P), intermediate radial diffusion (34% faster than struvite, 22% slower than KH2PO4), and increased bioavailable Ca reaching 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days (~8% recovery). The formation of hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2) was identified in soil conditions from 3 to 30 days, explaining the slower release trend. The study concludes that this mechanochemical approach yields an eco-friendly fertilizer that guarantees better nutrient management by playing on the solubility of Ca, K, and P, with no unwanted subproducts and no solvent waste. The work contributes to the current socio-environmental scenario by prioritizing environmental care using industrial and other potential wastes in the formulation of new products, avoiding unnecessary economic losses. A notable limitation is that the study did not report specific quantitative release rates or kinetic constants for all nutrients, and the bibliography appears to be omitted, which limits the ability to fully assess the theoretical foundations and reproducibility of the work. The absence of reported details such as the exact train/test analogs (here, precursor vs. milled samples), randomization of sample preparation, and complete characterization parameters in the main text also represents a gap, though the Supplementary Material is referenced for additional details. Overall, the study provides a reproducible framework for producing smart-release fertilizers from eggshell waste, with clear implications for sustainable agriculture and waste valorization.",

"title": "Mechanochemical synthesis of eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell (calcite) and KH2PO4",
"authors": "Roger Borges; Amanda Soares Giroto; Rodrigo Klaic; Fernando Wypych (Universidade Federal do Paraná); Caue Ribeiro",

"executive_summary": "This study presents an environmentally beneficial and cost-effective method of producing calcium phosphate bioceramics (potassium calcium phosphates) for soil conditioning, based on reverse logistics and green chemistry principles. The authors propose a free-solvent mechanochemical process between eggshell waste (calcite) and KH2PO4 to synthesize new phosphate phases, namely K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4, which provide better nutrient management of phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and calcium (Ca) when applied to soil systems. The material first releases K and forms hydroxyapatite, serving as an important P and Ca bioavailable source at pH ~5, which comprises a large part of many countries' soils. The research context emphasizes that reverse logistics is one of the most important instruments for applying shared responsibility for the product lifecycle, and eggshells are important wastes of food industries and excellent CaCO3 sources (more specifically calcite). The methodological approach involved collecting eggshells from the authors' homes, washing them with water, drying at room temperature, and grinding using a high-energy ball mill (Fritsch Pulverisette 7) with a 250 ml zirconia bowl and 5 zirconia balls of 15 mm diameter. The milling process was performed using a weight ratio of 1:1 (w/w) of eggshell and KH2PO4, first for 15 min, 30 min, 1 h, 2 h, 3 h, 6 h, 12 h, and 24 h at 600 rpm, and secondly at 100, 200, 400, and 600 rpm for 2 h. The mixture corresponds to 0.75 mmol of KH2PO4 and 1 mmol of CaCO3. After milling, the samples were characterized by X-ray diffraction (XRD), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) MAS, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC). The nutrient content was obtained by dissolving the samples using acid digestion in an H2SO4/H2O2 PA mixture (8:1 v/v, by 24 h at 250 °C), and determined by atomic absorption (K and Ca) and colorimetric (P) methods. The release essays were performed in citric acid solution (2 wt%), where the material was pelletized to simulate commercial products, with the pellets obtained in a steel pelletizer applying a pressure of 5 bar and the weight standardized to 100 mg/L of P. One single pellet was used in each essay in triplicate, placed in a 10 mL beaker immersed into 300 mL of 2% citric acid solution in a 600 mL beaker, kept closed with PVC film, in a constant temperature room at 25 °C under magnetic stirring. The phosphorus diffusion rates in soil were performed in Petri dishes containing moist soil, according to the method described by Degryse and Mclaughlin (2014), with each Petri dish having a diameter of 8.6 cm and 78 g of dry and sieved 2.0 mm mesh soil to achieve a density of 1.2 g/cm³. The key results show that the milling process between KH2PO4 and eggshell (98% of CaCO3) performed from 2 h and 400 rpm produces a mixture of phosphates, mainly K3CaH(PO4)2 and possibly CaKPO4. Below these milling parameters, only the reactants' diffraction patterns are found, indicating no evidence of chemical reaction. The TGA curve of KH2PO4 shows two main loss events: the first step at 200°C associated with crystallization water loss, and the second step at 300°C corresponding to polycondensation concomitant with structural water loss. The residual mass (89%) regarding KPO3 formation is consistent with the theoretical (87%). The thermal degradation of eggshell has two main steps: a first mass loss step below 300°C attributed to moisture elimination concomitant with organic membrane degradation, and a second step related to calcite decomposition below 700°C. For milled samples, three mass loss events are observed: the first step centered at 280°C related to crystallization water loss, the second step centered at 420°C associated with partial structural water loss and structure dimerization, and the final step centered at 710°C corresponding to final structural water loss reaction and structure polycondensation. The 31P NMR MAS spectra of the precursor KH2PO4 shows a single intense signal at δ = 3.74 ppm, characteristic of monosubstituted phosphate. The shift at δ = 3.28 ppm (2 and 6 h at 600 rpm) and at δ = 2.82 ppm (24 h at 600 rpm) are reported to calcium phosphates compounds, and the signal at δ = 0.74 ppm is related to disubstituted phosphate, suggesting H(PO4)2 5-species agreeing with the KCaPO4 formation. The kinetic study of the nutrient release was firstly evaluated in citric acid solution (2 wt%), and phosphorus and potassium release behavior were similar for the precursor (KH2PO4) and milled samples, but slower for milled samples, showing that the phosphates obtained by milling improve the nutrients management maintaining their bioavailability. For both nutrients, there was a substantial decrease of the kinetic constant from KH2PO4 to milled samples, attesting the delay in nutrient supply after mechanochemical processing. The temporal profile for the precursor KH2PO4 indicates a P increase from 0 mg/kg to 107 mg/kg after 3 days of release, keeping constant after 30 days, representing 40% of total P from precursor. Differently, for sample 2 h/600 rpm, the phosphorus release is more progressive (from 0 mg/kg to 25 mg/kg at 3 days and 45 mg/kg at 30 days) corresponding to 15% of total P content recovered from the milled sample. The P radial diffusion for the sample 2h/600rpm in soil reached a value of 1.99 cm, a significant value compared to 2.62 cm for KH2PO4, and struvite was not able to release any phosphorus at day 2. Results showed that the P radial diffusion profile from sample milled for 2h/600 rpm is intermediate, 34% faster than struvite and 22% slower than precursor at the end of 30 days. There is no increase in the bioavailable calcium when eggshell precursor (CaCO3) is applied in soil, but this concentration increases to 30.97 mg/kg after 30 days for 2 h/600 rpm sample, corresponding to around 8% of calcium recovery from sample. The interpretation and theoretical implications suggest that the slower release for calcium and phosphorus for 2 h/600 rpm sample and the P radial diffusion are probably related to hydroxyapatite formation, identified from 3 until 30 days in soil conditions. Hydroxyapatite is an important long-term calcium and phosphorus slow release fertilizer, turning systematically soluble by the natural soil pH acidification, especially under pH 5. The contradictions and limitations include the fact that below the milling parameters (time and milling speed), only the reactants' diffraction patterns are found, indicating no evidence of chemical reaction, and that all samples milled at 600 rpm do not present calcite decomposition below 700°C, but in samples milled for 2 h at 400 rpm this event is still observed, suggesting that low rotation speeds do not provide enough energy to degrade the total amount of calcite. The claims supported by evidence indicate that the mechanochemical process produces new phosphate phases such as K3CaH(PO4)2 and KCaPO4, which present a slower release character of potassium and phosphorus compared to the precursor KH2PO4, and a faster release character compared to the precursor CaCO3 from eggshell. The data and code availability is not reported, as the details of each characterization are described in Supplementary Material, and the soil properties are presented in Table S1. The robustness and ablation notes indicate that the milling process was performed to evaluate acid-basic reactions between the precursors to form potassium calcium phosphates. The ethical considerations are not explicitly reported, but the study is based on reverse logistics and green chemistry, using eggshell, a food industry residue, and KH2PO4 to design an eco-friendly fertilizer. The key figures and tables include Figure 1 showing the XRD patterns of the powders obtained after milling, Figure 2 showing the TGA curves, Figure 3 showing the calcined samples, Figure 4 showing the 31P NMR MAS spectra, Figure 5 showing the nutrient release behavior in citric acid solution, Figure 6 showing the nutrient release behavior in soil, and Figure 7 showing the hydroxyapatite formation. The top influential citations include Tibben and Lembke (2002), Byeon (2016), Kouznetsov et al. (2016), Jenkins et al. (1999), and Liu and Lal (2015). The three takeaways are: (1) the core contribution is the development of an eco-friendly fertilizer from eggshell and KH2PO4 using a free-solvent mechanochemical process; (2) the strongest evidence is the demonstration that the new phosphate phases delay the bioavailability of P and K while increasing the Ca bioavailability; (3) the future path is the use of the sample 2h/600rpm as nanocomposites to promote better solubilization of P and Ca when faster release is required.
